meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A Day Without Laughter Is a Day Wasted'?
meta.ogDescription: Chaplin never said it. The maxim is Nicolas Chamfort's, printed in 1795 — the Chaplin credit traces to a line in the 1992 film Shining Through.

answer.label: Not Charlie Chaplin — actually Nicolas Chamfort
answer.sourceLine: Chaplin never wrote or said this. The thought is a maxim by the French aphorist Nicolas Chamfort, printed posthumously from his manuscripts: Quote Investigator cites Mercure Français, 18 July 1795, p. 351, no. 60 ↗ for “La plus perdue de toutes les journées est celle où l’on n’a pas ri.” The compact eight-word English is nobody’s documented translation — period renderings read “the most lost of all days…” — and the Chaplin credit is traceable to a line of movie dialogue in the 1992 thriller Shining Through. Wikiquote files the line on Chaplin’s page under Misattributed ↗.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Mercure Français, 18 July 1795, p. 351, maxim no. 60 — posthumously, and the earliest printing located by Quote Investigator, which describes the paper as reprinting the saying from one of his manuscripts
French — “La plus perdue de toutes les journées est celle où l’on n’a pas ri.”
No standard one. The earliest English located by Quote Investigator is in Flowers of Literature; for 1801 & 1802 (1803); the popular eight-word form has no named translator.

source.excerpt: I admire the man who exclaimed, “I have lost a day!” because he had neglected to do any good in the course of it; but another has observed that “the most lost of all days, is that in which we have not laughed;” and, I must confess, that I feel myself greatly of his opinion.
trail: 1795 — Chamfort had died in Paris the previous year; the maxim reaches print from his manuscripts. Quote Investigator cites Mercure Français, 18 July 1795, p. 351, no. 60 ↗: “La plus perdue de toutes les journées est celle où l’on n’a pas ri.”

1803 — The saying crosses into English. QI’s earliest located English instance ↗ is in Flowers of Literature, which quotes it as “the most lost of all days, is that in which we have not laughed” and footnotes Chamfort’s French.

1887–1896 — The attribution is settled and correct on both sides of the Atlantic: an Edinburgh Philosophical Institution address names Chamfort as the author, and the 1896 Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations ascribes it to him in both languages ↗.

1992 — Chaplin’s name attaches. In David Seltzer’s Shining Through, released 31 January 1992 ↗, Melanie Griffith’s Linda Voss says the line and credits it to Charlie Chaplin: Quote Investigator quotes Joanna Connors’s Plain Dealer review of 31 January 1992, p. 5 ↗ — “Charlie Chaplin says a day without laughter is a day wasted,” says Linda Voss — the earliest Chaplin credit in QI’s chronology.
source.excerptNote: The earliest English-language instance of the aphorism that Quote Investigator located, in a section titled “Laughing.” The anonymous essayist does not name Chamfort, but an asterisk footnote at the foot of the page prints his exact French wording as the source of the English epigram.

source.rightsNote: Both documented sources are far older than any surviving copyright term. Chamfort’s French maxim was printed in Mercure Français on 18 July 1795, and the earliest English rendering appeared in Flowers of Literature; for 1801 & 1802 in 1803 — well before the 1931 US threshold, and their authors died in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The popular eight-word English phrasing has no identified translator or claimant, so no living rights attach to it either.

author.name: Nicolas Chamfort
author.kicker: The man who actually wrote it
author.heading: Nicolas Chamfort
author.bio: Born Sébastien-Roch Nicolas in Clermont-Ferrand in 1741, Chamfort made his name as a playwright and salon wit before the Revolution swept him up — he served as secretary to Louis XVI’s sister Madame Élisabeth, then, improbably, as secretary of the Jacobin club. He died in Paris in April 1794, and his reputation rests almost entirely on what he never published: the notebooks of epigrams gathered after his death as Maximes et Pensées, which John Stuart Mill admired and Sainte-Beuve compared to well-minted coins that retain their value. He was a professional compressor of ideas — which is exactly why a line of his survives two centuries later with somebody else’s face attached to it.

copyAttribution: "A day without laughter is a day wasted" is not Charlie Chaplin's. It is a loose modern English rendering of a maxim by the French aphorist Nicolas Chamfort (1741–1794) — "La plus perdue de toutes les journées est celle où l'on n'a pas ri" — printed posthumously from his manuscripts in Mercure Français, 18 July 1795, p. 351. The earliest English version located by Quote Investigator appeared in Flowers of Literature; for 1801 & 1802 (1803). The Chaplin credit traces to a line of dialogue in the 1992 film Shining Through. Source: Quote Investigator, quoteinvestigator.com/2011/07/16/laughter-day/

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and why they shouldn’t
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook magnet-name misattribution: a warm, quotable line about laughter drifting onto the most famous comedian of the twentieth century. There is no Chaplin source of any kind — no film, no interview, no page of his autobiography — and the credit is younger than the videocassette.

items.why: Wikiquote lists the line on Chaplin’s page under Misattributed ↗ and points to Chamfort. In Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ the first Chaplin credit is not Chaplin at all: it is a character in the 1992 film Shining Through, quoted in a Cleveland Plain Dealer review as saying “Charlie Chaplin says a day without laughter is a day wasted.”

The same line gets pinned on the other great comic name. Quote Investigator records a 2002 parenting book ↗ — Michael Gurian’s The Wonder of Girls, p. 167 — quoting a reader’s email whose second sentence runs “Groucho Marx once said, ‘A day without laughter is a day wasted.’” It is an attribution with no more evidence behind it than the Chaplin one.

Chamfort wrote a superlative, not a rule: “La plus perdue de toutes les journées…” — the most lost of all days. Wikiquote treats “A day without laughter is a day wasted” as a variant translation ↗, not as his sentence, and names no translator for it. Nobody has ever claimed authorship of this particular phrasing.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea belongs to Nicolas Chamfort, in French, printed from his notebooks in 1795, after his death the year before — and even then not in these eight words. Quote Investigator documents every step from 1795 to the movie line that made it Chaplin’s ↗.

context.heading: How a French misanthrope’s maxim became a Chaplin caption
lead: Chamfort was not a feel-good writer. The same 1887 Edinburgh address that credits him with this maxim also reports the lady who said a morning’s conversation with him left her melancholy until bedtime, and quotes his rule that whoever is not a misanthropist at forty can never have loved mankind. The laughter line was never a slogan for optimism; it was a bitter man’s note to himself, written in a notebook and published only after his death.

What made it Chaplin’s was a movie. In Quote Investigator’s chronology the saying circulates for nearly two centuries with no comedian attached — ascribed to Chamfort in an 1896 quotation dictionary, reworked without attribution in Ben Burroughs’s syndicated 1955 column “Sketches,” deployed by the founder of the National Laugh Foundation in 1979. Then in the 1992 spy melodrama Shining Through ↗, Melanie Griffith’s Linda Voss says the words out loud and puts Chaplin’s name in front of them. Quote sites did the rest.
context.detailsSummary: Why the eight-word version is nobody’s translation
detailsBody: Every documented English translation of Chamfort’s maxim before the twentieth century keeps his superlative construction. The 1803 Flowers of Literature has “the most lost of all days, is that in which we have not laughed”; the 1887 Edinburgh address has “the most wasted of all days is that on which one has not laughed”; the 1896 Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations has “the most completely lost of all days is that on which one has not laughed.” None of them is the line on the poster. The one pre-1900 loosening is not a translation at all: an 1880 essay on “Wit and Humour” by the Rev. W. A. O’Conor, in the Papers of the Manchester Literary Club, drops the superlative and paraphrases — “if he passed a day without laughing he should consider it a lost day” — which Quote Investigator presents as echoing Chamfort without naming him ↗. It is the closest ancestor of the compact modern form, and it still is not that form.

The compact modern phrasing surfaces only in the twentieth century, and not attached to anyone French: an index published in 1957 records an August 1956 article in the Soviet magazine USSR under the heading that Grigori Alexandrov says a day without laughter is a day wasted, and a 1979 wire obituary quotes laugh promoter George Q. Lewis saying “A day without laughter is a wasted day.” Wikiquote lists the eight-word form on Chamfort’s page as a variant translation ↗ rather than as anything he wrote.
context.pull: An aphorism by a man famous for making people gloomy, re-credited to the most beloved clown in film history.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces the saying to Nicolas Chamfort, citing Mercure Français, 18 July 1795, p. 351, no. 60 for 'La plus perdue de toutes les journées est celle où l'on n'a pas ri'; gives 1803 Flowers of Literature ('Laughing', p. 5) as the earliest English instance QI located; records the 1887 Edinburgh address and 1896 Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations crediting Chamfort; and gives the 1992 film Shining Through (Linda Voss / Melanie Griffith) as the Chaplin credit and a 2002 parenting book as the Groucho Marx credit. Re-checked 27 Aug 2026: QI says Mercure Français 'reprinted' the saying from one of his manuscripts (not that this was its first printing); cites 1880, Papers of the Manchester Literary Club, vol. VI, 'Wit and Humour' by Rev. W. A. O'Conor, p. 146 — 'Someone in later times said that if he passed a day without laughing he should consider it a lost day' — framed as 'a statement echoing the words of Chamfort without naming him'; cites the 1955 item as a signed syndicated column, 'Sketches' by Ben Burroughs (General Features Corp.), Gettysburg Times, 6 Dec 1955, p. 3, rewording the idea rather than quoting the saying; quotes the Groucho email as 'In our house, adventure and laughter go together. Groucho Marx once said, "A day without laughter is a day wasted." I always liked that comment.' from Michael Gurian, The Wonder of Girls (2002), p. 167; and cites the Chaplin credit to Joanna Connors, Plain Dealer, 31 Jan 1992, p. 5.

Wikiquote's Charlie Chaplin article lists 'A day without laughter is a day wasted' under its '== Misattributed ==' section, notes it is 'Widely attributed to Chaplin and a few others', points to Quote Investigator and to Chamfort's 1795 Mercure Français maxim, and reproduces the 1803 Flowers of Literature passage.

Wikiquote's Nicolas Chamfort article carries the maxim in its sourced section with the translation 'The most completely wasted of all days is that in which we have not laughed', lists 'A day without laughter is a day wasted' among 'Variant translations', and notes the Chaplin misattribution.

Wikipedia gives Chamfort's dates as 6 April 1741 – 13 April 1794, describes him as a French writer 'best known for his epigrams and aphorisms', secretary to Madame Élisabeth and of the Jacobin club, notes he worked for the Mercure de France, and lists Pierre Louis Ginguené's 1795 four-volume posthumous edition.
Wikipedia identifies Shining Through as a 1992 film directed and written by David Seltzer, released in the USA on 31 January 1992, starring Melanie Griffith as Linda Voss.

Google Books hosts the volume titled 'Flowers of literature; for 1801 & 1802(-1805): or, Characteristic sketches of human nature and modern manners' — the 1803 collection in which Quote Investigator located the earliest English instance of the saying.
